title: Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) - Network Theory Part 9

scenes.narration: Welcome back. In the parallel circuits part, we watched current split at a junction and join again, and the total always matched. That was not a coincidence. It is one of the two great laws of circuit theory, given by Gustav Kirchhoff in 1845. Today we learn the first: Kirchhoff's current law, usually called KCL. It works for every circuit ever built, however complicated, and it is the foundation of nodal analysis.
scenes.title: KIRCHHOFF'S CURRENT LAW
scenes.subtitle: What flows into a node must flow out

scenes.narration: Look at this node, where four wires meet. Watch the blue currents flowing in, and the orange currents flowing out. Five amperes and three amperes flow in. Two amperes and six amperes flow out. Now look at the total. In: five plus three is eight amperes. Out: two plus six is also eight amperes. The current flowing into a node always equals the current flowing out. That is Kirchhoff's current law.

Why must this always hold? Because charge cannot be created or destroyed, and a node is just a point of wire. It has no room to store charge. So every coulomb that arrives each second must leave in that same second. If more flowed in than out, charge would pile up at a single point, which never happens in a wire. KCL is simply conservation of charge, applied to a node. Think of water pipes joining: whatever water flows into the joint must flow out of it.
scenes.title: KCL = conservation of charge

parts.label: Charge can't be created or destroyed

steps.note: Like water at a pipe joint

scenes.narration: There are two ways to write KCL, and both mean the same thing. The first: the sum of currents entering equals the sum of currents leaving. The second: give currents entering a plus sign and currents leaving a minus sign, and then the algebraic sum of all currents at a node is zero. For our node: plus five, plus three, minus two, minus six, which is zero. Choose one sign rule and use it consistently for the whole problem.
scenes.formula: Σ I_in = Σ I_out     or     Σ I = 0

scenes.narration: Now let's use KCL to find a current we don't know. Four amperes and seven amperes flow into this node. Five amperes flows out through one wire. What flows out through the last wire? Think before the answer appears. In: four plus seven is eleven. Out so far: five. So the last wire must carry eleven minus five, which is six amperes, flowing out. Watch the label: six amperes out. KCL gave us the answer without measuring anything.

What if you don't know which way a current flows? Just guess. Draw an arrow in any direction, name it, and write KCL. If your answer comes out positive, the guess was right. If it comes out negative, the current simply flows the other way, with the same size. So a negative answer is not a mistake, it is information. This trick is used in every circuit analysis method.
scenes.formula: Assume a direction → solve → sign tells the truth
example: I = −2 A → 2 A in the opposite direction

scenes.narration: Let's check KCL in a real circuit. Here three resistors are in parallel across twelve volts. Watch the top junction. The source current, two hundred and twenty milliamps, flows into it. Out of it flow one hundred and twenty, sixty and forty milliamps. Add them: one hundred and twenty plus sixty plus forty is two hundred and twenty. Exactly what came in. At the bottom junction, the three currents join and return to the battery. KCL holds at every node.

KCL is even more powerful. It works not only for a single node, but for any closed boundary drawn around part of a circuit. Draw a circle around a group of components: the total current entering the circle equals the total current leaving it, because no charge can pile up inside. This idea is used later for the supernode, and it is also why the current entering a chip through all its pins must equal the current leaving it.
scenes.title: KCL for any closed boundary

parts.label: Draw a boundary around any region
Total current in = total current out

scenes.narration: Engineers use KCL every day. Nodal analysis, which we will learn soon, is nothing but KCL written at every node. When an electrician checks a house, the current in the phase wire should equal the current returning in the neutral. If it does not, some current is leaking, maybe through a person, and the RCCB in your home uses exactly this KCL check to cut the power in a fraction of a second.
scenes.title: KCL in practice

parts.label: Nodal analysis = KCL at each node

scenes.narration: Let's bring it together. Kirchhoff's current law: the total current entering a node equals the total current leaving it. Equivalently, the algebraic sum of currents at a node is zero. It comes from conservation of charge. If a current's direction is unknown, assume one, and a negative answer just means the opposite direction. And KCL also holds for any closed boundary.
scenes.title: KCL in one picture

scenes.narration: KCL is about current at a point. Kirchhoff's second law is about voltage around a path. In the next part we walk around closed loops, adding every rise and every drop, and discover why the total is always zero. That is Kirchhoff's voltage law.
scenes.title: NEXT: KIRCHHOFF'S VOLTAGE LAW
